c1ec407a6df510b1ef272075ca397e45cb387a16.summary: The page is titled as a report on CaddyWiper, a wiper malware said to target Ukrainian organizations, and carries an IBM byline. The body contains no threat content: only a long list of IBM-owned web properties, a source line and a page count. No actors, dates, tools, techniques, CVEs or figures appear in the text, so nothing can be recorded as a fact.

c133b079fdfe661f8e64e8d0ccf512f5668e1592.summary: Malpedia family page for the DarkSide ransomware. Its only description is a single sentence attributing a view of DarkSide as a C-written ransomware to FireEye. The rest of the page is an index of roughly 200 dated article titles, with vendor or media names and authors, about DarkSide and related ransomware groups. The page itself does not analyse a campaign, actor, or incident, so it is not treated as a threat report.

c113d860308817fd565d73657bc12da6d142c7bd.summary: FortiGuard Labs analysis of ELF/Sshdinjector.A!tr, a Linux malware collection injected into the SSH daemon. Samples surfaced around mid-November 2024 and the post says they are attributed to the DaggerFly espionage group. The collection includes a dropper, a malicious SSH library that communicates with a remote bot master and typically exfiltrates information, and persistence binaries. The post also evaluates using generative AI (r2ai with Radare2) for reverse engineering and notes hallucination, extrapolation and omissions in its output.

hedges: The DaggerFly attribution is cited from existing threat intelligence, and the post says nobody had examined what the samples actually do.
AI-generated analysis can hallucinate, extrapolate or omit details; the author says its output must be checked against a disassembler.
The author says AI-generated source code details are not always correct, while decompiler output is accurate but hard to read.
The author says the AI's claims that the malware manipulates the MAC address and hides its network communications are exaggerated.
